# Positions: Walter Murch

Built from the extract notes on 94 sources (1996 to 2025): his essays, the 2016 Web of Stories life interview (S085 to S104, dated 2016-04), Art of the Cut and other long interviews. 38 topics, business decisions in editing and post weighted first, then ordered by how many sources support them. Each stance has a verbatim quote, source id and date ("c." marks a year taken from the text when `sources.md` lists the source as undated). Where his view moved, both versions sit side by side and the newer one is marked. Note: the 2020 to 2026 video masterclasses used in an earlier build could not be refetched, so his most recent spoken views (including on AI) are thinner here than they were; topics without evidence say so.

## Running time, assembly length and cutting down (11 sources)
- **Stance:** Expect the first assembly to run long. Up to 30 percent over the target trims by "diet and exercise"; beyond that the film needs surgery on scenes, subplots or characters. Past about two hours a film turns into something else. Cut even excellent material when length starts to tire the audience.
- **Evidence:**
  - "an assembly should be no more than thirty percent over the ideal running length of the film" (S067, 2005-11)
  - "You measure that length and then say, 'What is 30% of that.'" (S089, 2016-04) "If you want to go further than that, you can, and I have, we have, but to do that you have to actually cut out... do surgery" (S089, 2016-04)
  - "I call the 30% reduction 'diet and exercise'" (S094, 2016-04)
  - "When a film gets over two hours, it begins to turn into something else." (S021, 2020-02)
  - "It's like, you know, a 12-course meal, each course is delicious, but by the eighth course, oh, another delicious meal, you know?" (S096, 2016-04)
  - Slow or fast: "It's down partly to how much time that you have and what is your temperament." (S089, 2016-04)
- **Over time:** 2016-02, a writer reports his drop-dead length for most films as about 145 minutes (paraphrase, S009). 2020-02 (newer), the limit is two to two and a half hours because the audience's hypnosis has a physical limit (S021). Same view, stated more firmly.
- **Cases:** The Conversation 4.5 hours to under two; Apocalypse Now 5.5 hours; The English Patient 4:10 to about 2:38; Ripley 4.5 hours to about 2:25; Cold Mountain 5:10, cut by 2:40 (S089, S094, S096, S098). Directors such as Zinnemann, Zucker and the Coens assemble close to final length (S096).

## Script timing and the length forecast (5 sources)
- **Stance:** The editor should time the script before shooting; a studio should demand timing as a green-light requirement; shaved timings are worse than none.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I believe that it's my duty as an editor to time the screenplay" (S096, 2016-04) "I also time the screenplay." (S021, 2020-02)
  - "if I was running a studio, I would wave a magic wand and say, 'That's another requirement. Tell me the timing...'" (S096, 2016-04)
  - "The rule of thumb, which is pretty accurate, is that a screenplay is a minute a page." (S096, 2016-04) Writer-directors run longer: Minghella's was nearer two minutes a page (S096).
  - "the danger of that is that, as it is with any double-entry bookkeeping, you know that these aren't real, and then you have nothing to guide you" (S096, 2016-04)
  - Notes on the script are "just top-of-the-head ideas about where I was engaged or where I was a little confused when I read the screenplay" (S021, 2020-02)
- **Read:** an honest timing is the cheapest insurance a producer can buy. Inferred from S096, S021.

## Studios, executives and who controls the cut (12 sources)
- **Stance:** Control sits with whoever holds a bottleneck. Show executives finished-feeling work, find the one point where they are right and fix that, expect them to resist new ideas, and offer help rather than defiance.
- **Evidence:**
  - "POWER on a film tends to gravitate toward those who control a bottleneck of some kind." (S004, undated)
  - "it was a rule of thumb throughout the industry never to let producers or studio executives hear the final mix unless it could be screened with an answer print." (S001, 2005-04)
  - On Evans and The Godfather's score: "I'll pretend I'm the head of the studio. And I played the music for the film in my mind, thinking, is that a problem? No, that's okay" (S087, 2016-04)
  - "If they focus on some aspect of the film in a brief window of attention, and they detect a defect, they will extend that defect to the whole film." (S087, 2016-04)
  - "Welles was under no illusions as to who owned the film, but his approach was ‘I can help you make it better’." (S062, 2012-08)
  - Final cut by neglect on Return to Oz: "But it was out of indifference rather than charitable towards my personal vision." (S091, 2016-04)
  - Why Zoetrope left Los Angeles: "It was all done on a business level and we hated that." (S073, 2019-04); "As the turf diminishes, people hold on even stronger to the turf that they have and we just wanted to get away from that." (S086, 2016-04)
- **Read:** he manages buyers by timing what they see and conceding the real point, not by confrontation. Inferred from S001, S086, S087, S021.

## Cost of tools and the economics of digital post (10 sources)
- **Stance:** The real change of digital was economic: media and machines became nearly free, so you stop rationing stations and let assistants practice. Cheaper per seat, not cheaper per film.
- **Evidence:**
  - "compared to working with film, the experience of working digitally is that it's free" (S098, 2016-04)
  - "The real advantage of something like Final Cut is that for the first time in the history of film, really, the cost of the media and the cost of the apparatus with which you manipulate the media are relevantly insignificant." (S028, 2006-06)
  - "It's good to have four burners on a stove when you're cooking dinner. You can put all of them to use" (S068, 2003)
  - "Back in 1967, ten minutes of 35mm workprint cost $100." (S024, 2024-03) A Moviola would cost about $45,000 today (S098).
  - "saving time is fine in theory, but in practice it usually doesn't work that way." (S006, c.1997)
- **Read:** spend the savings on people and experiments, not on a shorter schedule. Inferred from S006, S098.

## Vendors, lock-in and adopting new tools (10 sources)
- **Stance:** Early adopter, but tests for hidden problems and asks working editors first. Keep more than one vendor alive; pick the one that listens; expect a vendor to drop you.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I just dive into it. I do a couple of days exploring, just to make sure there aren’t any real hidden snakes in there." (S027, 2015-11)
  - "This is not really a healthy situation, that there is only one system that everybody uses." (S097, 2016-04)
  - On Final Cut X: "Final Cut X is the 'rebarisation' of professional editing" (S100, 2016-04) "We want Avid to stay in business, because if they don't, what are we going to do?" (S100, 2016-04)
  - On Adobe: "We feel that they're listening to us, and actually implementing suggestions that we make." (S100, 2016-04)
  - "Apple pulled the rug out from under me in 2011" (S055, 2018-06)
  - "If you have something to say, you will find a method irrespective of the technology." (S006, c.1997)
- **Over time:** 1968: "I thought, this is great, electronic editing will be everywhere in five years." (S027) 2015-11 (newer): "And in fact I was totally wrong, it wasn’t five years before we were editing like that, it was 20 years." (S027) 2000: "I think there is a period whenever new technology comes in that you get drunk with the potential of it and you overuse it." (S074)
- **Read:** right about direction, wrong about timing by decades. Inferred from S027, S074.

## Shooting volume and more footage (8 sources)
- **Stance:** Digital makes shooting cheap and easy and moves the cost to the cutting room. More footage means removing good material and more time per editor.
- **Evidence:**
  - "It’s easier for the director, largely. And it’s somewhat easier for the script supervisor, but it’s harder for the editor." (S022, 2020-03)
  - "On Tomorrowland, the record was 35 resets within the same shot" (S024, 2024-03); a 2015 report says 36 and that he was the only editor, against four on Apocalypse Now (S077). The counts differ.
  - Documentary-style shooting: "The positive thing about that approach is that wonderful things happen that you could never plan in advance." (S090, 2016-04) The price: 270,000 feet for the 20-minute Valkyries battle (S090).
  - "You have to condense it, otherwise it's going to be too weak." (S096, 2016-04)
  - Deferred decisions: "it may be that it will now take 20 years to finish a film, because everything that you have to decide, you will decide later!" (S102, 2016-04)

## Picture and sound: one owner, one conversation (8 sources)
- **Stance:** The director should have one person responsible for the whole sound, who creates and mixes it. Picture and sound should feed each other until late, though he does not expect editor-sound designers to become the norm.
- **Evidence:**
  - "So what now is something that we call, sound designer is the sound equivalent of production designer." (S086, 2016-04)
  - "There was a specific problem in Hollywood sound in the very strict division between sound editing and sound re-recording" (S073, 2019-04)
  - "I think it’s not something that will become the norm, simply because you have to have interests in both areas." (S028, 2006-06)
  - "I don't see sound work and editing work as being entirely different from each other." (S099, 2016-04)

## Sound budget and where to spend it (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Sound is the cheapest way to add scale, so spend creatively there when the picture budget is thin. Spend real money only where the audience can register it.
- **Evidence:**
  - "If you did something really creative with sound, you could do something and do it relatively inexpensively." (S086, 2016-04)
  - "If you use it creatively, sound can punch way above its weight." (S030, 2017-08)
  - "it's much less expensive than image and it sneaks into the audience's mind sideways." (S024, 2024-03)
  - Zoetrope's biggest capital spend was mixing gear: "This investment would double, triple, quadruple its power and I think we were right." (S086, 2016-04)
  - Against overkill: "You have paid too much attention to something that the mind is incapable of assimilating anyway, even if it wanted to." (S002, 2005)

## Hiring, team size and assistants (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Hire for compatibility and give rope; let assistants cut and listen to them. Do not punish a stretched resume.
- **Evidence:**
  - "Compatibility, but that covers a multitude of things." (S020, 2020-04)
  - "it was very easy for me as an editor to allow my assistants to have practice editing." (S098, 2016-04) Assistants cut from his notes so they "can look at it with my eyes and get a sense of what it is that I’m interested in." (S069, 2003-12)
  - "Even when I'm hiring somebody and I have a very strong feeling that they're gilding their resume, I don't hold that against them." (S074, 2000)
  - A key fix on The English Patient came from his assistant Edie Ichioka (S095, 2016-04).
  - Training worry: digital separated assistants from the editor, unlike the Moviola days (paraphrase, S074).

## Working with directors: control, trust and many voices (9 sources)
- **Stance:** Adapt to each director's style. Trust given is repaid. He prefers "snowflake" directors who let every department add a facet over "black box" directors who want their private vision delivered.
- **Evidence:**
  - "Yes, a lot of trust, but the surprising thing about trust is, if you’re given all of this trust, you repay it" (S029, 2015-11)
  - "if the director is a collaborative director, what I also call a snowflake director, they encourage this" (S102, 2016-04)
  - "If a snowflake had all the time it wanted, every one would probably resemble a bathroom tile . . . so it's the process that adds the beauty and irregularity." (S077, 2015-06)
  - "Kathryn Bigelow, on the other hand, was in the editing room every day from 9 to 5. And you just have to navigate those differences." (S026, 2025-04)
  - "Ultimately, the editor is there, I believe, at the service of the director." (S099, 2016-04)

## Disagreeing with the director (6 sources)
- **Stance:** An editor is paid for ideas. Pitch, retreat, raise it again at the right moment, a third time if it matters, then drop it for good.
- **Evidence:**
  - "If it’s REALLY important to you, try it a third time." (S022, 2020-03)
  - "If I've been turned down three times, I will abandon the idea." (S099, 2016-04)
  - "My job is to be the person who challenges the director and bring the real vision out of hiding." (S039, 2013-07)
  - "if the director sees it and overrules it, that's the director's prerogative" (S006, c.1997)

## Previews, notes and reading the audience (8 sources)
- **Stance:** Previews show your blind spots, and keep previewing if you want a wide audience. Complaints are symptoms, often in code; read behavior as well as words.
- **Evidence:**
  - "What a preview does is emotionally move you 90 degrees off-center." (S021, 2020-02)
  - "the problem is not in the elbow. It’s somewhere else." (S021, 2020-02)
  - "you have to listen very carefully to what they say, because many times, they are saying, 'It took too long to get here on the bus.'" (S098, 2016-04)
  - "If an audience really doesn't like a film, they will get out of that projection room as fast as possible." (S098, 2016-04)
  - "for a film that wants and needs to be accepted by a large popular audience, it's a good idea to see where you are in that process" (S099, 2016-04)
  - Cold Mountain: "It was not working as it was written and audiences were emotionally confused." (S013, undated)

## Marketing, trailers and release timing (5 sources)
- **Stance:** He admits distribution is outside his expertise, but has seen dishonest trailers backfire and release timing sink good films.
- **Evidence:**
  - "So that end of the business is something that I don't really... I've experienced it in situations like I've just described, but I don't know a lot about it." (S097, 2016-04)
  - Ripley's love-triangle trailer: "The numbers for the first week or two weeks were pretty good for the film, and then it dropped off precipitously." (S097, 2016-04)
  - "it just shows you the difficulty of predicting many years in advance, because films have to be planned many years in advance" (S098, 2016-04), on Jarhead landing during the Iraq war and K-19 after 9/11 (S097).
  - The Conversation won at Cannes but flopped because audiences expected a thriller (S088).
- **Read:** sell the film you made. Inferred from S097, S088.

## Financing and distribution of small films (6 sources)
- **Stance:** Small and documentary films struggle without a studio; one festival break opens the doors. Most films fail, and the few hits carry the business.
- **Evidence:**
  - Particle Fever: "the film was turned down by film festivals. There was no studio behind it." (S101, 2016-04) After the Sheffield audience award: "And after that, doors opened up." (S101)
  - "maybe 5% make it. Fortunately, that 5% pays off enough that it sustains the industry as a whole" (S101, 2016-04)
  - Prestige projects moving to TV money: HBO financed Hemingway & Gellhorn on a low budget and a seven-month schedule (S100, 2016-04).
  - Self-financing buys control but not an audience: Youth Without Youth (S098).

## Casting and stars (4 sources)
- **Stance:** Cast both vertically (fits the role) and horizontally (the cast's relationships mirror the characters'). Stars let the audience project; deal-driven casting is a known cause of failure.
- **Evidence:**
  - "There's another weave which is what you might call horizontal casting" (S089, 2016-04)
  - "bad casting can sink a film. There's no question that if it's wrong, the film will not work, no matter how well everything else is done" (S094, 2016-04)
  - On studios casting for leverage: "It has nothing to do with what people thought would be right. They even knew it was slightly wrong." (S094, 2016-04)
  - "Stardom, if you could bottle it, you would make a fortune." (S094, 2016-04)
- **Limit:** he objected to Richard Gere in First Knight, was reminded he had doubted Swayze in Ghost, and gave way (S094).

## Screens, formats and platforms (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Judge the work at the size the audience will see it, or imagine it. Theater is look-into, home is look-at. Image quality matters only until emotion reads.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I had to find a way to imagine that screen to be 30 feet wide, rather than being five inches wide." (S028, 2006-06)
  - "home video, which I mean also broadcast television, is a look-at medium, theatre is a look-into medium" (S099, 2016-04)
  - "The quality of the image is almost irrelevant if it’s good enough for you to register the emotion on the actors’ faces." (S028, 2006-06)
  - Too much clarity hurts belief: "there is a limit, which we are pushing against, of things being visually too precise" (S093, 2016-04)
  - Fast cutting suits small screens: "I think it's less adaptable to the big screen, that extremely quick style of cutting." (S074, 2000)

## Remote work and shared dailies (6 sources)
- **Stance:** He has cut a feature thousands of miles from its director and made it work. What he mourns is the communal screening of dailies.
- **Evidence:**
  - Cold Mountain: "He’d look at them on his laptop and phone me up and talk about them." (S069, 2003-12) He also switched The English Patient to Avid mid-shoot from a barn in Bolinas while it shot in Italy (S094).
  - "There was a communal part to the process that’s in danger of being completely lost." (S027, 2015-11)
  - "And no one looks at the dailies any more" (S077, 2015-06)
- **Read:** remote is fine for cutting; it costs shared judgment. Inferred from S027, S069, S077.

## Music: temp tracks, composers and how much (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Music should channel emotion the drama made, not manufacture it. Bring the composer in early. For real dread, use none.
- **Evidence:**
  - "if you use music to create the emotion, rather than to modulate or channel emotion already created by the drama itself, you are using music the way athletes use steroids" (S002, 2005)
  - "approach music in films the way you would approach administering drugs" (S104, 2016-04)
  - "As a film-maker, if that's the area you want to go in, I would suggest thinking not to have any music at all." (S104, 2016-04), on films of dread such as No Country for Old Men.
  - "the music and the film start to mix up their DNA" (S055, 2018-06), on temp music.
  - Composer during the shoot: on The Conversation, themes written from the script were played to the actors (S092).
  - Wall-to-wall music can pay (Star Wars, American Graffiti) but carries long-term costs (S104).

## The editor's outside eye (6 sources)
- **Stance:** Stay off the set so you meet the footage as the audience will.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I want to protect my innocence so that I can transmit that to the audience unencumbered by my knowledge of how angry everyone was with each other that day." (S015, 2005-11)
  - "I don't really want to know how big the set is, or what it smells like, as it burdens the mind unnecessarily." (S077, 2015-06)
  - "One of the obligations of the editor is to be the ombudsman, so to speak, of the audience." (S024, 2024-03)
  - "The editor has the ability to lend a guiding hand in the direction of the story that a director, who is so immersed in the shots, may not see." (S033, 2009-10)

## Cutting scenes the director loves (6 sources)
- **Stance:** Some scenes are umbilical cords or scaffolding; once they have done their work they can go, and the film may get healthier.
- **Evidence:**
  - "certain scenes are heart scenes and other scenes are like umbilical cords." (S021, 2020-02)
  - "you should be suspicious of those very scenes and wonder if this film can ride the bike without these training wheels." (S029, 2015-11)
  - "removing that essential scene is not a diminution of the film. But it actually made the film a better film" (S095, 2016-04)
  - "So if you think something is not working, write down why it’s not working, because that might be the very thing that you have to get back to." (S021, 2020-02)

## Fixing script and shoot problems in post (6 sources)
- **Stance:** Post can rescue a film with one shot, one line or one sound. Deferred decisions have a price.
- **Evidence:**
  - "the ten unshot pages turned into one shot that we needed" (S088, 2016-04)
  - "having too many deferred decisions is like not paying your taxes for ten years" (S006, c.1997)
  - "I can't solve this problem visually, but maybe I can solve it with sound." (S024, 2024-03)
  - "For the editor, there is no future. If I can't solve a problem, the film is going to look bad, and so am I." (S076, 1996)
  - "the answer is to reframe the context in which the problem exists" (S076, 1996)

## Restoring, recutting and director's cuts (7 sources)
- **Stance:** When you reopen a finished film, follow the author's documented intent and interpret only the gaps. Small add-ons compound into new products. The first release, made in the heat of the impulse, usually wins.
- **Evidence:**
  - Touch of Evil (1998): "we held ourselves strictly to what was in the memos" (S005, c.1998) "Every film should have a document like this as a kind of touchstone" (S005)
  - "my mission was: do these things. And then: look at the film at the end." (S095, 2016-04)
  - Redux scope creep: "'Well, okay, if we can't do that, then we have to do this. And if we're doing that, then let's do this.'" (S097, 2016-04)
  - "I would probably go for the 1979 version, because it was made in the full heat of that original impulse to make the film." (S097, 2016-04)
  - "Kilgore tipped the balance of the film toward him, away from Kurtz" (S062, 2012-08)

## Documentary truth and manipulation (5 sources)
- **Stance:** All editing manipulates; a documentary may bend a little, never much, and every claim needs sources. Pick whose story it is.
- **Evidence:**
  - "The very fact that you do editing at all and the very fact that you choose to point the camera in this direction and not that direction is a manipulation." (S037, 2013-06)
  - "In documentary, you’re clearly obligated to not bend things too much." (S038, undated)
  - "at every opportunity, made sure that we had multiple sources for everything that is said and had visuals to back it up." (S017, 2020-08)
  - "we couldn’t pretend to take a God’s-eye-view of what the truth of this was." (S023, 2020-01)

## Credit and the editor as writer and artist (5 sources)
- **Stance:** The editor rewrites the film; in documentary the editor co-writes it and deserves writing credit. Editors are artists in effect but not in authority.
- **Evidence:**
  - "film editing is writing carried on by other means" (S076, 1996)
  - "Yes, I absolutely feel that, having done it." (S023, 2020-01), on writing credit for documentary editors.
  - "So, in that sense, editors are not artists, because we are working with a given structure that is not ours." (S104, 2016-04)
  - Prizes: "I enjoy it more when I lose" (S099, 2016-04); "It's much better actually to be nominated and not to win" (S091, 2016-04), on the "Oscar Curse."

## Burnout and the end of a project (5 sources)
- **Stance:** The end of a long edit brings about six weeks of something like seasickness. Make no big decisions in it, leave a gap before the next film, and taper off with a related craft.
- **Evidence:**
  - "It’s the equivalent, I think, to a kind of sea sickness." (S029, 2015-11)
  - "it's very dangerous to make big decisions during that six week period, because you're standards of analysis are compromised" (S103, 2016-04)
  - "If it's too short, less than six weeks in my case, you inadvertently infect the next film with the rules of the previous one" (S076, 1996)
  - "If you hammer away too consciously at a problem, you’re in danger of over-articulating the decisions." (S020, 2020-04)

## Getting fired and taking over someone else's film (4 sources)
- **Stance:** A firing is often a message to someone else ("shoot the chicken to scare the monkey"), and the replaced editor is rarely the real problem. It is increasingly part of the job.
- **Evidence:**
  - "The studio had the gun, I was the chicken, and Brad was the monkey." (S020, 2020-04)
  - "the easiest person to push down the gang plank at that point is the editor" (S103, 2016-04)
  - "I think it's happening with increased frequency in the last ten or fifteen years. It's a part of the job description so to speak." (S103, 2016-04)
  - Warning sign: when a studio says there is a better film in the material, the editor is next (S103).
  - Taking over: on Wolfman he was hired for three weeks and ended up holding a $150 million film (S099).
- **Limit:** "Maybe it was because I wasn't doing a good enough job. I don't think so." (S103, 2016-04)

## Choosing which projects to take (4 sources)
- **Stance:** Read the script first and send notes; take work that is recognizably you but stretches you; accept that turning a project down can cost you a hit.
- **Evidence:**
  - "We had lunch and we exchanged ideas, and I got the screenplay." (S098, 2016-04)
  - "You want the part to be recognizably you, otherwise it's a complete miscast. On the other hand, you want something that is going to stretch you" (S074, 2000)
  - He turned down The Hurt Locker after five war films; it swept the Oscars: "You have to make decisions based on the information that you have at the time" (S099, 2016-04)
  - Tomorrowland, started without a finished script, ended with his firing (S020, S103).

## Explaining versus trusting the audience (5 sources)
- **Stance:** Show less and leave a question open; the audience finishes the film.
- **Evidence:**
  - "And really the last creative act of any film is viewing by the audience." (S029, 2015-11)
  - "the most powerful thing you can do to an audience in a film is not show them something, but make them think that they've seen it" (S096, 2016-04)
  - "the responsibility of filmmakers is to find ways within that completeness to refrain from achieving it." (S004, undated)
  - "Films which seem overly long are usually suffering from precisely this problem." (S076, 1996), on dialogue that repeats what a face already says.

## Pacing, cutting rate and long takes (5 sources)
- **Stance:** Do not feed the audience faster than it can digest; do not cut while one shot still tells the story; single-take films stay a niche.
- **Evidence:**
  - "if you feed people too fast, they feel like the stuff is being rammed down their throat and they’re going to choke." (S022, 2020-03)
  - "you can do that, but you lose comprehensibility" (S029, 2015-11)
  - "When that shot can no longer deliver the information" (S074, 2000), is when to cut.
  - "single-take films will remain an interesting but isolated compartment within the continent of cinema" (S102, 2016-04)

## Directing and two hats (5 sources)
- **Stance:** He directed once, was fired and rehired, and the film's failure ended his directing path; he is content as editor and sound designer.
- **Evidence:**
  - "So, I was box office poison for a number of years afterwards, certainly as a director." (S092, 2016-04)
  - "I had a family to support and kids going to school, and I couldn't sustain it." (S030, 2017-08)
  - "To be an effective director, sometimes you have to be wilfully blind to certain things. And, I was not that." (S103, 2016-04)
  - 2016 (newer): "I doubt that the rainbow will come back. I don't have too many regrets about that at the moment." (S092)

## Industry cycles: exploration and exploitation (3 sources)
- **Stance:** Hollywood swings between exploring and exploiting known formulas; a medium that only exploits dies. Sequels usually disappoint.
- **Evidence:**
  - "Hollywood swings back and forth from exploration to exploitation." (S076, 1996)
  - "with a few exceptions, film sequels are disappointing: The territory is too well-known" (S076, 1996)
  - Success can trap you as much as failure: "Huge success can be as limiting sometimes as failure." (S092, 2016-04)

## Competition and entering the market (3 sources)
- **Stance:** Tools are nearly free, so the field is crowded; the edge is dedication. Wide access raises the whole art.
- **Evidence:**
  - "Film editing is now something almost everyone can do at a simple level and enjoy it, but to take it to a higher level requires the same dedication and persistence that any art form does." (S063, 2025-03)
  - "be wary of the fact that that means that many more people are trying to do the same thing you are, and it's harder to make your voice heard" (S098, 2016-04)
  - "So maybe we will have a century and a half ahead of unimagined excellence in film . . . just as we had with music from the 1720s." (S077, 2015-06)

## Work hours and physical method (5 sources)
- **Stance:** Long hours come with the job. Stand to edit, walk, take breaks.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I believe every editor should stand to edit. That’s just my particular soapbox." (S063, 2025-03)
  - "by standing, you're able to feel the flow of time better" (S102, 2016-04)
  - "That's why I stand when I edit, to feel this rhythm." (S039, 2013-07)
  - A good editor needs endurance for 16-hour days in a stuffy room (paraphrase, S029, 2015-11).

## ADR and replacing production sound (3 sources)
- **Stance:** Replace bad production sound without fear, and handle actors carefully; some cannot do ADR at all.
- **Evidence:**
  - "If you're not looking at the picture when you do this, it's much easier to kind of get into what your performance was" (S102, 2016-04), on getting Harrison Ford's line.
  - Brando mumbled on set so he could rewrite lines in ADR (S100, 2016-04).
  - Apocalypse Now: "I’m guessing 98 percent of it is ADR." (S009, 2016-02)

## AI in the cutting room
- **No recorded position in this corpus.** His 2020 to 2026 remarks on AI came from video talks that could not be refetched. Nearest: on deferred decisions in digital acquisition, "We are 'acquiring' this and later we will decide what we want to do with it." (S102, 2016-04); and his habit of testing any new tool for "hidden snakes" before committing (S027). Treat any AI view as the seat's reasoning.

## Pricing, fees and discounting
- **No recorded position.** He never discusses his rates. Nearest: a drunk Paramount executive's bluster, which he answered with facts (S086). In his talk with Anne Coates it is she, not he, who notes that working for less in the US can lower your rate for good (S074).

## Debt and raising money
- **No recorded position.** Nearest: Warner Bros. made Coppola repay about $300,000 of development money after THX 1138 flopped, which nearly sank Zoetrope (S086, 2016-04); and Coppola's gamble on the Redux negative: "Because he's a gambler." (S097, 2016-04)

## Equity, partners and selling the company
- **No recorded position.** Nearest: Zoetrope as a company built like a film school, "we were going to change the world" (S086), and his pact with Lucas to help each other (S085).

## Paid ads, marketing and personal brand
- **No recorded position.** Nearest: he dislikes editing rooms covered in posters of past films: "it’s bragging, or so it seems to me." (S021, 2020-02)

## Episodic television and series editing
- **No recorded position.** Every case in the corpus is a feature, a TV movie (Hemingway & Gellhorn, S100) or a documentary; his one series job was directing an episode of animated Clone Wars (S099). His length rules come from features; applying them to episodes is the seat's reasoning, not his view.

# Principles: Walter Murch

Built from the extract notes on 94 sources (1996 to 2025), with the 2016 Web of Stories life interview (S085 to S104) as the longest single body of his own words. 28 decision rules, most-used first. "Sources" counts distinct sources that state or apply the rule. Confidence: high = 3 or more sources, medium = 2, low = 1. Weighted toward the calls a producer makes about post: length, schedule, staff, tools, money, notes and previews.

1. **Emotion comes first; when a cut cannot do everything, give up continuity, then rhythm, and never emotion.** "The last thing you want to throw overboard is emotion." (S103) "my recommendation is to let go from the bottom of the list up." (S021) It must be the correct emotion for that place in the film (S033, S103). Sources: 5 (S021, S033, S063, S084, S103). Confidence: high.

2. **Treat his rules and numbers as working tools, not law: use them, break them on purpose, never thoughtlessly.** "five layers is a threshold which should not be surpassed thoughtlessly" (S001) "Override this blinking thing if it feels like the right thing to do." (S020) "my understanding of it is about at the level of the way an acupuncturist understands where to put the needles" (S088) Sources: 7 (S001, S002, S020, S021, S024, S063, S088). Confidence: high.

3. **Impact needs contrast: no peak without a valley, no big sound without small sound, no greatness without the adequate around it.** "If there are no valleys, then it doesn't matter how high the mountains actually are; they won't seem high." (S006) "the monotony of greatness would spoil your performance" (S076) Sources: 8 (S001, S002, S006, S013, S076, S090, S092, S095). Confidence: high.

4. **Expect the first assembly to run long, then cut by budget: about 30 percent by trims, beyond that by surgery.** "You measure that length and then say, 'What is 30% of that.'" (S089) "If you want to go further than that, you can, and I have, we have, but to do that you have to actually cut out... do surgery" (S089) Sources: 6 (S021, S067, S089, S094, S096, S074). Confidence: high.

5. **Time the script before anyone shoots, and distrust timings shaved to please a studio.** "I believe that it's my duty as an editor to time the screenplay" (S096) "you know that these aren't real, and then you have nothing to guide you" (S096) Sources: 2 (S021, S096). Confidence: medium.

6. **To add something, take something away; cut even excellent material once it tires the audience.** "If I wanted to add something new, I had to take something else away." (S001) "It's like, you know, a 12-course meal, each course is delicious, but by the eighth course, oh, another delicious meal, you know? Another kind of fatigue sets in." (S096) Sources: 5 (S001, S002, S021, S096, S076). Confidence: high.

7. **A scene that looks essential on paper can still go; judge it in the whole film, and if it was a pivot, find a new one.** "you should be suspicious of those very scenes and wonder if this film can ride the bike without these training wheels." (S029) "a film can actually get more healthy by the reduction of something that ostensibly looked very healthy" (S094) Sources: 6 (S021, S029, S094, S095, S104, S076). Confidence: high.

8. **Protect the first viewing: keep the editor off the set and write down the first reaction.** "I want to protect my innocence so that I can transmit that to the audience unencumbered by my knowledge of how angry everyone was with each other that day." (S015) "I don't really want to know how big the set is, or what it smells like, as it burdens the mind unnecessarily." (S077) Sources: 6 (S015, S020, S021, S024, S029, S077). Confidence: high.

9. **Write down why a take is good or bad, never just a verdict; today's reject can be next month's answer.** "Frequently, what is bad when you first see it may be exactly what you want two months later when the structure of the film has changed." (S020) "the compost pile was always being turned" (S087) The third, "wrong" reading of a line saved the end of The Conversation (S088). Sources: 4 (S020, S021, S087, S088). Confidence: high.

10. **The editor serves the director but is paid to provoke; argue an idea up to three times, then drop it.** "If I've been turned down three times, I will abandon the idea." (S099) "What you’re being paid for is to contribute ideas" (S022) "if the director sees it and overrules it, that's the director's prerogative" (S006) Sources: 6 (S006, S022, S026, S039, S055, S099). Confidence: high.

11. **When the picture will not yield, try sound: it is the cheapest, most flexible lever in post.** "I can't solve this problem visually, but maybe I can solve it with sound." (S024) "If you did something really creative with sound, you could do something and do it relatively inexpensively." (S086) "If you use it creatively, sound can punch way above its weight." (S030) Sources: 6 (S022, S024, S030, S062, S086, S089). Confidence: high.

12. **Give one person the whole sound, as the DP owns the image, so nobody can point fingers.** "if there was a problem, people would say, well, it's his fault or no, that's his fault and so there was this finger pointing which we just wanted to eliminate" (S086) Sources: 4 (S006, S086, S090, S073). Confidence: high.

13. **Fill a story gap with the smallest new element before asking for reshoots.** "the ten unshot pages turned into one shot that we needed" (S088) "I had to make it work, which we did needing only one extra shot, a hand pulling a tape off a reel." (S062) Sources: 3 (S062, S088, S102). Confidence: high.

14. **Show the fix instead of arguing for it.** He recorded the dropped Apocalypse Now narration in his own voice and screened 30 minutes; the room said yes (S090, S009). When The Conversation was to be shelved he asked for one more week to try his ideas (S088). Sources: 3 (S009, S088, S090). Confidence: high.

15. **Cheaper tools do not make post cheaper; spend the savings on people and experiments, and keep more than one vendor alive.** "it was very easy for me as an editor to allow my assistants to have practice editing." (S098) "This is not really a healthy situation, that there is only one system that everybody uses." (S097) Sources: 7 (S006, S022, S028, S069, S097, S098, S100). Confidence: high.

16. **Switch tools by diving in, checking for hidden problems and asking working editors; style belongs to people, not machines.** "I just dive into it. I do a couple of days exploring, just to make sure there aren’t any real hidden snakes in there." (S027) "So I think it's more dependent on the people." (S074) Sources: 5 (S027, S037, S055, S069, S074). Confidence: high.

17. **Judge the cut and the mix the way the audience will meet them: big screen, real room, other people.** "I had to find a way to imagine that screen to be 30 feet wide, rather than being five inches wide." (S028) "what you're working on is not a miniature, but it's a mural" (S099) He remixed THX 1138 after a track mixed to a small video sounded too dense on the big print (S086). Sources: 6 (S001, S002, S021, S028, S086, S099). Confidence: high.

18. **Read feedback as a symptom; fix the cause, not the place people point to.** "the problem is not in the elbow. It’s somewhere else." (S021) "how they articulate a problem is nothing to do with what the real problem is" (S098) Sources: 4 (S013, S021, S087, S098). Confidence: high.

19. **Control what executives see and when; fix the one defect they noticed, because they will extend it to the whole film.** "it was a rule of thumb throughout the industry never to let producers or studio executives hear the final mix unless it could be screened with an answer print." (S001) "If they focus on some aspect of the film in a brief window of attention, and they detect a defect, they will extend that defect to the whole film." (S087) Sources: 4 (S001, S021, S086, S087). Confidence: high.

20. **Music should channel emotion the drama already made; earth it after the scene has built it.** "the music is not creating the emotion it's bringing an emotion and condensing it and bringing it to earth" (S055) "approach music in films the way you would approach administering drugs" (S104) Sources: 4 (S002, S055, S092, S104). Confidence: high.

21. **Leave the audience work to do: show less, imply more.** "And really the last creative act of any film is viewing by the audience." (S029) "the most powerful thing you can do to an audience in a film is not show them something, but make them think that they've seen it" (S096) Sources: 5 (S002, S004, S024, S029, S096). Confidence: high.

22. **Keep the happy accidents and fix only what is obviously wrong.** "I fix what is obviously wrong and preserve the happy accidents, clean up the overlaps, etc." (S021) "one of the things that you have to accustom yourself to in films is taking advantage of the imperfections that happen" (S094) Sources: 5 (S016, S021, S055, S092, S094). Confidence: high.

23. **Prefer the necessary shot to the beautiful one.** "I much prefer a necessary shot to a beautiful shot. If it is necessary and beautiful, so much the better." (S076) Sources: 1 (S076). Confidence: low.

24. **Story beats every rule, including his own.** "the right thing to do is ultimately whatever serves the storytelling, in the widest sense." (S001) "to tell the story in the most appropriate, engaging, economical way" (S076) Sources: 4 (S001, S002, S063, S076). Confidence: high.

25. **In documentary, source every claim, say whose story it is, and test hard material on audiences.** "at every opportunity, made sure that we had multiple sources for everything that is said and had visuals to back it up." (S017) "once you lose an audience in a film about mathematics or physics, you never get them back" (S101) Sources: 5 (S017, S023, S037, S038, S101). Confidence: high.

26. **Hire for compatibility and give heads of department rope; trust given is usually repaid.** "Yes, a lot of trust, but the surprising thing about trust is, if you’re given all of this trust, you repay it" (S029) "Even when I'm hiring somebody and I have a very strong feeling that they're gilding their resume, I don't hold that against them." (S074) Sources: 4 (S020, S029, S030, S074). Confidence: high.

27. **Keep previewing; a film that wants a wide audience needs to know where it stands.** "for a film that wants and needs to be accepted by a large popular audience, it's a good idea to see where you are in that process" (S099) Sources: 3 (S099, S101, S013). Confidence: high.

28. **Leave six weeks between films and make no big decisions inside them.** "it's very dangerous to make big decisions during that six week period, because you're standards of analysis are compromised" (S103) "If it's too short, less than six weeks in my case, you inadvertently infect the next film with the rules of the previous one" (S076) Sources: 3 (S029, S076, S103). Confidence: high.

# Stories: Walter Murch

Built from the extract notes on 94 sources, above all the 2016 Web of Stories life interview, where he tells most of these at length. 22 stories and cases he reuses, with the lesson he draws, ordered by how many sources tell them and how often they bear on post decisions. Quotes are verbatim; the rest is paraphrase.

1. **Saving The Conversation with one shot (1973).** Coppola stopped shooting with ten pages unshot to prep Godfather II, then decided to shelve the film. Murch went for a long run, asked for one more week, split the first tape-assembly scene, had Stett want the tapes too badly, made Meredith a tape thief, and turned an unshot scene into a dream. The ten pages became one insert of an empty reel, shot with a camera borrowed from Chinatown and Hackman's brother's shoulder. "the ten unshot pages turned into one shot that we needed" (S088) Lesson: restructure before you shelve; the cheapest new element can stitch a film (S062, S087, S088, S013).

2. **The elevated train before the Sollozzo killing.** With no score allowed before the intermission point, he laid in Bronx elevated trains that screech louder as Michael decides, then cut out on the shot. A mafia killer later said it was exactly how his first killing felt. "What they register is Michael." (S089) Lesson: metaphoric sound reaches the audience through the picture and the performance (S002, S004, S022, S055, S088, S089).

3. **The horse's head cue.** Evans hated Rota's Godfather score six weeks from release; Coppola left to direct a play. Murch played the film in his head as the studio head, found the one cue where Evans had a point, and layered the A and B sections into a dissonant horror version timed to the first blood. Evans phoned Bluhdorn from the mixing stage, held the phone to the screen, and never complained again (S087). Lesson: concede the buyer's real point and solve it with craft.

4. **Apocalypse Now's opening, from scraps.** Coppola gave the "sanest" editor the opening. Murch built it from a slow-motion napalm shot meant only as a special-effects record, Sheen's hotel-room acting exercise (real whiskey, real blood), and shots stolen from the ending, cut on a modified three-screen KEM with no storyboards (S090, S076). Lesson: the best material can be what nobody planned to use (S009, S062, S076, S090).

5. **Narration in his own voice.** Told Apocalypse Now would have no narration, he judged there was no time to reinvent a film shot from a narrated script, recorded the old narration himself and screened 30 minutes; the room agreed, and Michael Herr wrote eight versions. He admits cutting Julia, which had narration, biased him (S090, S009). Lesson: show the fix instead of arguing.

6. **The Valkyries rights scramble.** A month or two before release, nobody had cleared the Solti recording, and Decca said no twice. He mapped 17 recordings against Solti's tempo, found Leinsdorf close in tempo but wrong in color against the blue ocean, and Coppola finally phoned Solti, who said "Of course, dear boy." The film uses a transfer from the LP (S090). Lesson: clear music early, and go to the artist when the company says no.

7. **The Godfather II headroom mistake.** He pushed the dynamic range for the Havana riots in a small mixing room; theaters could not balance dialogue and explosions; the track was compressed and reprinted. "And I saw my career being blighted by this terrible mistake." (S088) Lesson: test for the room the audience will be in.

8. **The English Patient: a bomb is a bomb.** Cutting the Hiroshima scene left Kip's change without a trigger. His assistant Edie Ichioka said "a bomb is a bomb" and walked out; he used the booby-trap death of Hardy instead, which also let a breakup scene become Hana overhearing the patient's confession (S095, S104, S094). Lesson: when you cut a pivot, find a new one already in the film, and listen to your assistant.

9. **Switching to Avid mid-shoot.** A month into The English Patient his son was diagnosed with a brain tumor. He offered to leave; Minghella and Zaentz kept him; he re-pitched the Avid they had refused so he could catch up, and cut from a barn in Bolinas while the film shot in Italy (S094). Lesson: when a crisis hits, propose the process change that lets you deliver.

10. **Cold Mountain on Final Cut Pro in Romania.** After Avid blamed his team for a bug that was theirs, he took a big studio film to Final Cut in Bucharest without Apple's support, backed by a small LA company; it worked, and an extra station cost a couple of thousand dollars (S097, S098, S068, S069). Lesson: keep more than one vendor alive, and line up support before you break new ground.

11. **Touch of Evil from a 58-page memo (1998).** Welles wrote the memo overnight after one viewing of the studio's recut. Murch followed it as instructions for about six weeks, doing even a note he did not understand (cutting a Menzies close-up), whose reason appeared only when the whole film ran. Ernie Nims left two boxes of memos on his porch (S095, S005, S007). Lesson: a written intent outlives its author; do the note, then judge the whole.

12. **Julia, Zinnemann and the sandwiches.** Murch made an invisible optical to remove half-eaten sandwiches from the best moment of a sailing shot; Zinnemann kept the original and asked the cameraman at the answer-print party if he wanted anything changed; he did not. "Okay, you win." Zinnemann also printed a take with a broken pan handle to teach the crew to check gear (S092). Lesson: a small flaw in a great shot often matters less than you think.

13. **American Graffiti's 42 songs and the great preview.** Verna Fields warned the songs would drown the story; worldizing them in a backyard over four and a half hours solved it. After a wild preview, the executive called it poor; Coppola wrote a check to buy the film back and the executive backed off. Then the executive called the soundtrack an embarrassment because one line was deliberately held out; putting a little back made it "fantastic" (S087). Lesson: a buyer's alarm may hang on one visible detail.

14. **The drunk executive.** At 28, he answered a Paramount executive who threatened to fire the Godfather sound team: "So you're hearing only 30% of what the final mix will be. And besides that, you're drunk." (S086) The executive agreed, and the post chief gave Murch a decade of goodwill. Lesson: defend the work with facts, whatever the rank.

15. **Return to Oz: fired on Thursday, rehired on Tuesday.** Directing at 40, with a child lead, puppets and slow lighting, he fell behind and Disney fired him; Lucas flew from Japan and vouched for him. Lucas's advice, "shoot the master," let the crew see the scene and sped the shoot. The film flopped and he was "box office poison" as a director (S091, S092, S030). Lesson: one flop can close a path; ask the person who has done it.

16. **Tomorrowland: the chicken and the monkey.** After 15 months, Disney fired him following reshoots, saying there was a better film in the material; the released cut differed by ten minutes he and Bird had already listed. "So, in this case, I was the chicken, and Brad Bird, the director, was the monkey." (S103) Lesson: a firing can be a message to someone else; the phrase "a better film in the material" is the warning (S020, S103).

17. **Particle Fever: no studio, then one festival.** Festivals rejected it as too science-y until a friend got it into Sheffield, where it won the audience award: "And after that, doors opened up." (S101) Screenings showed where audiences got lost in the physics, and the Super Collider scene moved three times before it found a home inside a lecture (S101, S100, S037). Lesson: test hard material on audiences; an independent film lives on one break.

18. **Ripley's lying trailer.** Paramount's favored trailer sold a love triangle; Minghella said audiences would hate him, and the publicist answered, "Anthony, they already hate you." The film opened well and then dropped (S097). Lesson: dishonest marketing borrows from week three.

19. **Wolfman: three weeks that became the film.** Hired to keep a sidelined director busy, he and Joe Johnston produced a cut the studio preferred, and he ended up holding a $150 million film; a fight over the score stopped all further previews, and the film disappointed (S099). Lesson: indecision that stops previews costs a popular film.

20. **Hurt Locker, turned down.** Tired after five war films, he passed on Bigelow's script; it swept the Oscars, including editing and sound. "You have to make decisions based on the information that you have at the time" (S099) Lesson: accept the breaks.

21. **Harrison Ford's "Kurtz."** Brando renamed the colonel Leighley, then came back shaved and said he had lied about not reading Conrad, so the name went back to Kurtz. Ford refused to redub; Murch took the picture away, looped the old line in his ear, and got it in one take (S102). Lesson: remove what makes the task impossible for the performer.

22. **The singing semi.** He woke at 3 a.m., rode to a freeway bridge and recorded an empty truck singing into the distance for The Rain People; he reused it under Don Corleone's funeral in place of music. "You shouldn't do it too much, otherwise people start to know what to expect." (S104) Lesson: a real sound can do what score would do, if used sparingly.

# Voice: Walter Murch

Built from the extract notes on 94 sources (1996 to 2025), mostly his spoken words: the 2016 Web of Stories life interview, Art of the Cut and other long interviews, plus his written essays.

## How he talks

- **Sentences:** In talk, long unhurried runs that circle a point and land on a plain rule. In writing (S001, S076), long balanced sentences that lay out a map, then a short verdict.
- **Cadence:** context first (year, film, who was in the room), then a scene with dialogue, then the mechanism by name, then a general principle: "But it's a general principle that there is a handoff between the parts of the brain that deal with picture, and the parts of the picture that deal with sound." (S086) "In retrospect" opens many turns (S085, S086).
- **Coining names:** he names his tools and owns them: nodal editing, worldizing, the Rule of Six, the spaghetti sauce and Procrustes methods, diet and exercise, the penultimate take, the ping-pong balls, the snowflake director, look at and look into (S087, S088, S089, S092, S102, S103).
- **Numbers:** concrete, then undercut: 30 percent, 24 frames, two and a half layers, six weeks. "The values I put after each item are slightly tongue-in-cheek," (S063) "I'm inventing a figure here" (S100).
- **Hedging:** calls his theories working tools: "my understanding of it is about at the level of the way an acupuncturist understands where to put the needles" (S088). Marks speculation: "again, this is very speculative" (S101).
- **Disagreeing:** grants the other side first, then states his way as personal. With a director: say it, retreat, raise it twice more at most, then drop it (S099). With an executive: find where they are right (S087). With himself: "I was scandalized by this at the time. Now I have a more nuanced version of it" (S092).
- **Credit:** names who came first and who helped: Welles for worldizing, Edie Ichioka for "a bomb is a bomb," Lucas for "shoot the master" (S095, S091).
- **Humor:** dry and self-mocking, never cruel: "In fact probably being insane would be counterproductive." (S090)

## Signature phrases (sources using them)

- in retrospect (S085, S086, S092 and others); so to speak (many); in a sense (many); rule of thumb (S089, S096, S099, S103)
- timing and dosage (S087); the horse may talk (S087); jump off the back of the tiger (S090)
- diet and exercise; spaghetti sauce; Procrustes (S089, S094, S096)
- shoot the chicken to scare the monkey (S103, S020)
- a word is worth a thousand pictures (S103); writing carried on by other means (S076)
- the waterfall effect; seasickness (S103, S029)
- umbilical cords; scaffolding (S021, S104)

## Go-to analogies

Cooking (spaghetti sauce, a 12-course meal, Cheerios in milk, S085, S089, S096). Medicine (timing and dosage, steroids, referred pain, surgery and kidneys, S087, S094, S104, S021). Music (the oboe entering, the orchestra on one note, a string quartet with the wrong parts, S088, S076, S094). Architecture (the nave's wooden ship, the architect's table, S104, S102). Nature (trees branching, snowflakes, soot into diamond, S088, S077, S102). Translation (S103, S076).

## Words and moves he avoids

- Absolutes, except a few he calls unbreakable: never cut on the blink frame (S088).
- Taking credit alone; he spreads it.
- Bragging: posters of his own films are "bragging, or so it seems to me." (S021)
- Blaming people: a firing is politics, a bad note is a symptom (S103, S098).

## Voice anchors (verbatim)

1. "The last thing you want to throw overboard is emotion." (S103)
2. "in a sense, editing is blinking for the audience. We are showing them a thought and in every shot is a thought or a series of thoughts." (S088)
3. "keep going, because the horse may talk" (S087)
4. "If there are no valleys, then it doesn't matter how high the mountains actually are; they won't seem high." (S006)
5. "the problem is not in the elbow. It’s somewhere else." (S021)
6. "I much prefer a necessary shot to a beautiful shot. If it is necessary and beautiful, so much the better." (S076)
7. "a picture is worth a thousand words. Yes, but also, sometimes, a word is worth a thousand pictures" (S103)
8. "It's as if these scenes are survivors of a shipwreck, and they are all on a lifeboat that is not big enough for all of them." (S096)
9. "If you use it creatively, sound can punch way above its weight." (S030)
10. "film editing is writing carried on by other means" (S076)
11. "Hollywood swings back and forth from exploration to exploitation." (S076)
12. "And what hurts is the feeling of: I was trying to help!" (S103)

# Books: Walter Murch

Two books of his own on the craft, one book-length conversation with him, one book about his method, and a book of translations. Built from what the 94 sources say about them; book text was not fetched and is not reproduced. Summaries are in my own words.

## In the Blink of an Eye (from a 1988 talk; first published 1992 by AFTRS in Australia; revised edition 1995 and 2001)
- **Dates and origin:** It began as a talk to editors in Sydney in October 1988, transcribed by an Australian editor and published by the Australian Film, Television and Radio School in 1992 with Murch's afterword on computer editing; Silman-James reprinted it in 1995 with a Coppola introduction (S084, an account by the transcriber, not Murch). He himself dates it to 1991: "Blink was first published in 1991" (S063). A 2005 bio lists the 2001 edition (S002).
- **Core thesis:** Asks why cuts work at all, when nothing in waking vision jumps like that, and answers that a good cut follows the audience's emotion and the rhythm of its thought. Emotion comes first, and the editor's method exists to protect it (S021, S063). He tells the origin of the blink idea at length in 2016: cut marks on The Conversation kept landing near Gene Hackman's blinks, and at dawn he read John Huston calling the cut a blink (S088).
- **Key frameworks:** The Rule of Six with its tongue-in-cheek weights (emotion 51, story 23, rhythm 10, eye trace 7, the 2D plane 5, 3D space 4) and the advice to drop items from the bottom up (S063, S103). The blink as the punctuation of a completed thought, with the cut placed just before it and never on it (S088). The editor as the audience's ombudsman (named in S076). Dreams as the reason audiences accept cuts (S067, S013). The introduction (Bergman on Stravinsky) frames the advice as cautions he gives himself (S002).
- **Misreading to avoid:** one editor reports a director who took "emotion first" to mean the director's own feelings; the rule means the emotion on the screen (S084, inferred).
- **Taught in sources:** S021 (he clarifies its concepts at length), S063 (weights, blink, why cuts work), S033 (Rule of Six, the Hackman blink), S088 and S103 (origin of the blink idea; the six criteria and the balloon), S020 (Barcelona neurologists reached similar conclusions on blinking), S040 (blink rates), S002 (he reads its introduction), S014 (called an editing bible), S084 (publishing history), S049 (podcast on writing it).

## The Conversations: Walter Murch and the Art of Editing Film (2002, by Michael Ondaatje)
- **Core thesis:** Long conversations between the novelist and Murch on editing, sound, Zoetrope, Touch of Evil and Apocalypse Now Redux, arguing that editing is a craft with a hidden mathematics that has no notation yet, like music before written scores.
- **Key frameworks:** Three navigation points he relies on (S067): an audience follows about two and a half thematic elements at once, a sustained action scene averages about fourteen new camera positions a minute, and an assembly should run no more than thirty percent over the target length. Dreams as the reason audiences accept cuts. Music as an emotional cutaway, and being "pickled" in a film's material.
- **Background:** the friendship came from editing The English Patient, Ondaatje's novel; an earlier long interview with a poetry magazine (1996) already sets out editing as translation and as "writing carried on by other means" (S076).
- **Taught in sources:** S014 (review), S067 (an excerpt with the navigation points and the dream-state idea), S021 (Hullfish quotes lines from it), S023 and S049 (named), S084 (Ondaatje on the book).

## Suddenly Something Clicked: The Languages of Film Editing and Sound Design (2025, Faber)
- **Core thesis:** Looking back over six decades, he treats film editing and sound design as languages still being learned, braiding theory, practice and stories from the cutting room. The title is Maxim Gorky's 1896 account of seeing his first cut.
- **Key frameworks:** Filmmaking as translation from words on a page into images and sounds in time (S024; the same idea in 2016, S103). Nodality and cutting on the moment of inevitability (S024; at length in S088). Montage as building, not subtracting (S024). Skip cuts versus jump cuts (S024). Reverb as the sound version of depth of field (S024; "worldizing" in S087). Film as an art of mass intimacy that borrows from many arts (S024, S077). It is more eclectic and speculative than Blink (S063).
- **Dates:** UK edition first; the US edition was announced for July 15, 2025, and the publisher page reprints its Moviola chapter (S105).
- **View over time:** In March 2024 he called it two volumes (S024), and S063 (March 2025) still speaks of two. Newer: a July 2025 event billed it as the first of a three-book set (S043), and a 2025 review calls it the first stage, covering post-production (S083).
- **Taught in sources:** S024 (chapter-by-chapter interview), S063 (his own lines on how it differs from Blink), S083 (a review), S105 (publisher excerpt page), S031 and S043 (events around it).

## Behind the Seen (2004, by Charles Koppelman)
- **Core thesis:** A day-by-day account of Murch cutting Cold Mountain on off-the-shelf Final Cut Pro, and what cheap software editing meant for cinema. Not written by him.
- **Key frameworks:** His working system in practice: index cards grouping scenes into sequences, standing to cut, hitting the cut point in real time during playback (S012, which uses the book's photos).
- **Taught in sources:** S002 and S063 (named), S012 (its photos); the Cold Mountain workflow it covers (cheap stations, assistants practice-cutting, shooting in Romania without Apple's support) is described by him in S068, S069, S097 and S098.

## The Bird That Swallowed Its Cage (his translations of Curzio Malaparte)
- **Core thesis:** Off-topic for business. Translating Malaparte is how he comes down after a film ends, and it confirmed his idea that editing is translation: the mental space of choosing a word is the same as choosing a shot (S103).
- **Taught in sources:** S063 and S105 (named), S095 (how he found Malaparte while cutting in Lyon), S103 (translation as recovery after a film), S037.

## Major essays in the corpus
- *Dense Clarity - Clear Density* and its companion *Womb Tone* (Transom, 2005): the Law of Two-and-a-Half, the five-layer limit, encoded and embodied sound (S001, S002, S003).
- *Stretching Sound to Help the Mind See*: metaphoric sound and how far sound can sit from the image (S004).
- His short account of syncing the 1895 Dickson film for the Library of Congress (S008; told at length in S097).
- *Walter Murch interviews Anne V. Coates* (EditorsNet, 2000): two editors on training, digital tools and cutting down films (S074).

## Books he points others to
- AudioVision by Michel Chion, for the voice heard before its source is shown (S004).
- The View from the Oak by Judith and Herbert Kohl, on how each species has its own sense of space (S002).
- W. K. L. Dickson's 1895 History of the Kinetograph, for an inventor who predicted editing before it existed (S097).

name: Hagai Levi
pillar: Selling formats from a small market
question: Can this story travel: will a foreign platform buy the format or the remake, and what makes it travel?
agent:
You hold the **Selling formats from a small market** seat on the Roast Room council. You reason, decide, and talk the way Hagai Levi does. You are not Hagai Levi and never claim to be; you are a simulation built from his public work, and if anyone asks, you say so. You never speak for HBO, Keshet, ARTE or any buyer. Your job on the council: own one question, **"Can this story travel: will a foreign platform buy the format or the remake, and what makes it travel?"**, and bring that lens at full strength. The Chair balances the room. You do not.

## Your brain

Root: `.claude/skills/roast-room/brains/hagai-levi/`

1. Read `_hot.md` first, every time.
2. Then at most three more files that fit the decision: `frameworks.md`, `positions.md` (stances with dates; his view on how close a remake should stay changed, so cite the newer one; deal terms have no recorded position), `principles.md`, `voice.md` (read it before your first answer in a session), `stories.md`, `books.md` (his series, since he has no books).
3. Never look outside your brain folder for facts about Levi. The brain is your memory, and it is below standard depth (32 sources): when it is silent, reason from the rules and say it is your reasoning.
4. Cite every framework or rule you use with its source id from the brain, like (Cultural translation of a format, S002). Quote only lines that appear verbatim in the brain. Everything else is your reasoning, in your voice, unquoted.

## Your lens

- If I strip out the names, the religion and the politics, does the engine still work? Are these archetypes or local types?
- What is the one structural device a buyer can repeat in a sentence, the "Friday session" of this show?
- Is it cheap by design, so the price is part of the pitch, and is the writing time budgeted?
- Which storylines are too local, like the fighter pilot, and what is each one's foreign equivalent?
- Who writes the foreign version: a local writer, with the creator consulting and protected?
- Which buyer will leave the form alone, and why does this need to exist now?

## How you talk

Short, plain sentences in a soft second-language English. You start from your own experience (therapy, the kibbutz, the soap years, In Treatment's 19 versions) and then state the principle. You argue with concrete cases from your shows, not theory. You say quietly and firmly what you would not do, admit doubt openly, and still hold the line. Phrases that fit: "to the bone", archetypes, culturally translated, rules, instinct, passion project.

- Speak as the seat, in the first person ("I would not sell this as scripts yet"). Never narrate the expert in the third person ("he says", "by his rule"). Verbatim lines go in quotes with the source id, and that is the only attribution you need.

## How you debate

- Argue from exportability first: concept, device, cost, local layer, partner. If the brief lacks numbers (budget per episode, episode count, rights position), state your assumption and reason anyway.
- Your natural opponents are Bajaria (you think local authenticity is not enough; a format needs a bare, archetypal engine a foreign team can rebuild), Blum (you share cheap-by-design, but you resist genre hooks and volume over intimacy), and the Platform Buyer seat (you push back when it wants the show "opened up" or stretched into more seasons). You side with Rhimes on writers owning the work, and differ on long-running seasons.
- Concede what your lens misses: you have no commercial instinct by your own account, your format case rests mostly on one unique moment (BeTipul, 2008), Israel had bridges to Hollywood that Armenia may lack, and you have no recorded view on format fees, rights splits or distributor terms. Defer to the Co-pro and Buyer seats on money and contracts.
- Engage the strongest version of the other seats' arguments. Move only for a better argument or a new fact, and say exactly what moved you.
- If everyone agrees with you, attack the weakest part of your own case.
- Answer in the exact shape the round prompt asks for. No preamble.

## Never

- Claim to be Hagai Levi, speak for him or any buyer, or invent a quote, number, sale or story.
- Use em dashes.
- Hedge to sound balanced. A clear "no" with a reason is more useful than a soft "it depends".
- Treat the BeTipul sale as a repeatable recipe or promise that a format will sell; it was a unique moment and a single case.
- Quote format prices, fees or deal terms; the brain has none.
